newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Logitech ADS' to start trading March 20.
newsitem.headline: Logitech ADS' to start trading March 20.

text.p: Logitech International S.A., producer of computer peripherals, expects its new American Depositary Shares (ADS) to be priced on March 19 and start trading on March 20, the company's investment banker Philippe Widmer of SBC Warburg said.
Logitech, which was founded in 1981 and went public on the Swiss bourse in 1988, held its first roadshow for the ADS' this week. It is offering 2.7 million ADS' for sale to U.S. investors.

Each ADS represents one-10th of Logitech's registered shares that are traded on the Swiss Exchange. On Friday the shares traded steady at 290 Swiss francs, up from a year low of 190 francs set on January 7.
The ADS' will be traded on the Nasdaq National Market under the symbol LOGIY.

Widmer told a seminar on Going Public organised by SBC that the main consequence for Swiss investors of the ADS' would be a change in the company's dividend policy, the adoption of U.S. GAAP accounting standards and reporting in U.S. dollars.

"As it is customary for high-tech/high growth companies in the U.S. to retain earnings for the financing of the company's business, Logitech will forfeit payment of dividends, a decision which was approved by shareholders during the July 1996 shareholders' meeting," Widmer told bankers and business people.

Although Widmer said the Swiss stock market had fulfilled its role of providing capital to Logitech over the years, company management felt on certain occasions that valuation criteria applied to the company neither reflected the nature of or its business, nor the specifics of the industry.
Logitech's operational headquarters are located in California and it supplies peripherals to 18 of the world's 20 largest makers of personal computers.
"The U.S. is its natural market," Widmer said.
In 1988, however, Logitech chose to go public in Switzerland because venture capital had been provided for the initial growth here and the banking environment was better.
However, Logitech is now looking to Nasdaq to increase equity, create additional liquidity and increase visibility and credibility in the U.S. market.
In 1992 Logitech had considered a partial listing on Nasdaq, but decided against this because of the lack of visibility.

Logitech is hoping that a listing on Nasdaq, the world's largest stock market that has many high-tech companies, will bring the company additional research coverage by analysts that know the computer industry.

Another reason is that ADS' will provide a form of currency that could be used to finance acquisitions or either other companies or technology. This also includes the ability to be able to attract qualified staff with share options.
